title: Fasting Fuel and Its Failures: Gluconeogenesis, von Gierke, Galactosaemia, Reducing Sugars and Lactic Acidosis
summary: Learn how glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis share fasting glucose supply, why glycogen storage disease type I blocks both, how classical galactosaemia presents and why galactose is stopped on suspicion, which sugars reduce copper, and how lactic acidosis is defined and typed.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 17 Hits 11–15. Checked against Gerich 2010, Froissart 2011, Welling 2017 (GalNet guideline), Rubio-Gozalbo 2019, Coelho 2017, Succoio 2022, Hernández-López 2020, Zanza 2022 and See 2024 (all full text via Europe PMC; no page-fetch tool used). Hit 11 calls GSD Ia the only GSD affecting both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; Froissart 2011 attributes the block to the whole glucose-6-phosphatase system, so GSD Ib (translocase) shares it (register flag rv-gsd1-ib-shares-block). Hit 12 names Q188R without population context; Coelho 2017 notes it is the most common variant in people of European ancestry and that Asian populations are understudied (register flag rv-galt-q188r-population). Hit 13 gives a single >5.0 mmol/L lactate cut-off; Zanza 2022 states definitions vary and uses >4 mmol/L (register flag rv-lactic-acidosis-cutoff). Hit 14 frames early fasting as glycogenolysis followed by gluconeogenesis with a ~12–24 h glycogen supply; Gerich 2010 gives about half of glucose from gluconeogenesis already after an overnight fast and virtually all by 48 h (register flag rv-fasting-gng-overlap). Not taught (pending): the 12–24 h glycogen supply figure, the “oil-drop” description of galactosaemic cataracts, the Clinitest brand name, the anomeric-carbon explanation for sucrose, and the 45 mg/dL lactate figure.

objectives: Describe how glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, in liver and kidney, supply glucose during a fast.
Explain why glycogen storage disease type I causes fasting hypoglycaemia with high lactate, lipids and urate, and recognise classical galactosaemia and its immediate management.
Identify reducing and non-reducing sugars in copper-reduction testing and classify lactic acidosis as type A or type B.

scenes.title: Three broken fuel lines
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three patients — (1) a 4-month-old with a protruding abdomen, hypoglycaemia a few hours after a feed, high lactate and very high triglycerides; (2) an 8-day-old drinking milk, with vomiting, jaundice, Escherichia coli in the blood culture and urine positive for reducing substances; (3) an adult taking metformin, with acute kidney injury, normal blood pressure, no hypoxia, pH 7.29 and lactate 6.0 mmol/L. Question token: “Which fuel line broke?”

cues.text: An invented morning. A four-month-old with a swollen belly becomes hypoglycaemic a few hours after a feed, with high lactate and very high triglycerides.
An eight-day-old on milk is vomiting and jaundiced, grows E. coli in the blood, and has reducing substances in the urine. An adult on metformin has a lactate of six with a pH of seven point two nine.
Three patients, three broken fuel lines. Which line broke in each?

scenes.title: How a fasting body keeps glucose up
scenes.altText: Schematic timeline of fasting glucose supply (Gerich 2010). After a 14–16-hour overnight fast, glucose is released at about 10 μmol/kg/min: roughly half from liver glycogenolysis and half from gluconeogenesis in liver and kidney, from lactate, glycerol, alanine and other amino acids. The liver supplies about 75–80% and the kidney 20–25%; the kidney releases glucose only by gluconeogenesis because it holds very little glycogen. Lactate is the main gluconeogenic precursor in both organs. As fasting continues, liver glycogen is depleted; by 48 hours virtually all glucose released comes from gluconeogenesis. Glucagon stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.

cues.text: Between meals the blood still needs glucose. After an overnight fast, about half comes from breaking down liver glycogen, glycogenolysis.
The other half is new glucose made by gluconeogenesis, from lactate, glycerol, alanine and other amino acids. Lactate is the main starting material.
Gluconeogenesis runs in the liver and the kidney. The kidney supplies about a fifth of fasting glucose, and only by gluconeogenesis, because it stores very little glycogen.
As the fast goes on, liver glycogen runs down. By forty-eight hours, virtually all the glucose comes from gluconeogenesis.

scenes.title: Two inborn blocks: GSD I and galactosaemia
scenes.altText: Left card: glycogen storage disease type I (von Gierke). The glucose-6-phosphatase system hydrolyses glucose-6-phosphate to glucose — the last step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Type Ia: catalytic unit G6Pase-alpha (about 80% of GSD I); type Ib: glucose-6-phosphate translocase, with neutropenia. Excess glucose-6-phosphate drives hyperlactataemia and hyperlipidaemia, with hyperuricaemia (reduced renal urate clearance as lactate competes, plus increased urate synthesis); hepatomegaly, doll-like face; glucagon gives no glucose rise and worsens lactate. Right card: classical galactosaemia (GALT deficiency). Newborns exposed to milk develop feeding difficulty, vomiting, jaundice, liver damage with bleeding, Escherichia coli sepsis and cataracts. Start a galactose-restricted formula (soy-based, casein hydrolysate or elemental) immediately on suspicion, without waiting for confirmation; confirm by red-cell GALT activity and/or GALT gene analysis.

cues.text: Glycogen storage disease type one, von Gierke disease, breaks the glucose-six-phosphatase system. That system makes the very last step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, so both fuel lines fail.

Type one A lacks the enzyme itself; type one B lacks the transporter that carries glucose-six-phosphate to it, and adds neutropenia. Trapped glucose-six-phosphate drives up lactate and triglycerides, and uric acid rises too. Glucagon raises lactate, not glucose.
Classical galactosaemia is a deficiency of the enzyme GALT. Once a newborn drinks milk: vomiting, jaundice, liver damage with bleeding, E. coli sepsis and cataracts.
Treat on suspicion: start a galactose-restricted formula immediately, without waiting for confirmation. Confirm with red-cell GALT activity or GALT gene testing.

props.title: GSD I (von Gierke)
lines: G6Pase system: last step of BOTH

scenes.title: Reducing sugars, lactate, and the hook
scenes.altText: Card 1: copper-reduction (Benedict-type) testing — in alkaline solution, reducing sugars with a free carbonyl group (glucose, fructose, lactose, maltose) reduce Cu2+ to Cu+ (Cu2O); sucrose is non-reducing and stays negative. Urine reducing substances can point to galactosaemia but are also positive in prematurity, renal tubular acidosis, some drugs and other metabolic diseases. Card 2: lactic acidosis — definitions vary; one review uses lactate >4 mmol/L, bicarbonate <20 mmol/L and pH <7.35; metformin-associated lactic acidosis is confirmed at lactate >5 mmol/L with a high-anion-gap acidosis. Type A: low tissue oxygen delivery (septic, cardiogenic, hypovolaemic, obstructive shock). Type B: no hypoperfusion — B1 disease (for example liver disease), B2 drugs or toxins (metformin), B3 errors of metabolism. Hook answers: (1) GSD I; (2) galactosaemia — stop galactose now; (3) type B (B2) lactic acidosis from metformin.

cues.text: At the bench, a copper-reduction test turns positive with reducing sugars: glucose, fructose, lactose, maltose. Sucrose is non-reducing and stays negative. A positive urine points toward galactosaemia but is not specific.

Lactic acidosis: lactate up with acidaemia. Cut-offs vary between sources: one review uses lactate above four, bicarbonate below twenty and pH below seven point three five; metformin cases are confirmed above five, with a high anion gap.
Type A comes from poor oxygen delivery, as in shock. Type B has no hypoperfusion: a disease such as liver disease, a drug such as metformin, or an inborn error.
Back to the hook. The infant has GSD type one. The newborn has galactosaemia, so galactose stops now. The adult has type B lactic acidosis from metformin.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “GSD Ia is the only glycogen storage disease that blocks both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis” (✓ GSD Ib, a translocase defect in the same glucose-6-phosphatase system, blocks the same last step); “Wait for the GALT result before stopping milk” (✓ start a galactose-restricted formula immediately on suspicion); “Glycogen alone feeds the first day of fasting” (✓ after an overnight fast gluconeogenesis already supplies about half the glucose).

cues.text: Trap one: only type one A blocks both pathways. No: type one B, a transporter defect in the same glucose-six-phosphatase system, blocks the same last step.
Trap two: wait for the GALT result before stopping milk. No: start a galactose-restricted formula as soon as galactosaemia is suspected.
Trap three: glycogen alone feeds the first day of a fast. No: after an overnight fast, gluconeogenesis already supplies about half.

props.title: ✗ “Only GSD Ia blocks both pathways.”
lines: ✓ GSD Ib (translocase) blocks the same last step

scenes.title: One exit door
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Glucose-6-phosphatase is the liver’s single EXIT DOOR. The glycogen WAREHOUSE and the gluconeogenesis FACTORY both ship glucose through it. Lock the door (GSD I) and the backed-up stock spills into lactate, fat and urate.” Tokens: warehouse = glycogen · factory = gluconeogenesis · door = G6Pase. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: glucose-six-phosphatase is the liver’s exit door. The glycogen warehouse and the gluconeogenesis factory both ship through it. Lock the door, and the backed-up stock spills into lactate, fat and uric acid.
Where it breaks: the kidney also makes and releases glucose; type one B is a broken conveyor to the door, not the door itself; and a few patients tolerate fasting better than the picture predicts.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Overnight fast ≈ half glycogenolysis, half gluconeogenesis · GSD I locks the last step of both”, “Galactosaemia: stop galactose on suspicion · sucrose is non-reducing · lactic acidosis type A = shock, type B = disease, drug, inborn error”.

cues.text: After an overnight fast glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis share the work, glycogen storage disease type I blocks the last step of both, suspected galactosaemia means stopping galactose at once, sucrose does not reduce copper, and lactic acidosis is type A with shock and type B without it.

props.label: Fast: glycogen + GNG · GSD I blocks the last step of both
Galactosaemia: stop now · sucrose non-reducing · lactate A vs B

explanation.what: Plain language: between meals the liver keeps blood sugar up by emptying its glycogen store and by making new glucose; the kidney helps by making new glucose. Some inherited enzyme defects break this supply (von Gierke disease) or make a milk sugar toxic (galactosaemia). Lactate, a product of glucose breakdown, builds up and acidifies the blood when oxygen delivery fails or when disease, drugs or inborn errors interfere. Scientific terms: glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis, gluconeogenic precursors (lactate, glycerol, alanine, glutamine), glucose-6-phosphatase system (G6Pase-alpha, glucose-6-phosphate translocase), glycogen storage disease type I (Ia, Ib), galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT), Gal-1-P, reducing sugar, copper reduction (Benedict reaction), hyperlactataemia, lactic acidosis type A and type B (B1, B2, B3), D-lactic acidosis.
explanation.why: Glucose-6-phosphatase hydrolyses glucose-6-phosphate to free glucose at the last step of both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, so a defect in its enzyme (Ia) or translocase (Ib) blocks both; excess glucose-6-phosphate is diverted to lactate and lipid production, and uric acid rises because lactate competes for its renal clearance and urate synthesis increases. In GALT deficiency, galactose from milk accumulates as galactose-1-phosphate and galactitol (cataracts), so removing dietary galactose resolves the acute neonatal illness. Reducing sugars with a free carbonyl group reduce Cu2+ to Cu+ in alkaline solution; sucrose does not.
explanation.measure: Overnight (14–16 h) fast: ≈10 μmol/kg/min glucose release, ≈50% glycogenolysis, ≈50% gluconeogenesis; liver 75–80%, kidney 20–25%; by 48 h virtually all gluconeogenesis. GSD I: fasting hypoglycaemia with hyperlactataemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercholesterolaemia, often hyperuricaemia; glucagon after fasting gives no glucose rise and raises lactate. Galactosaemia: start galactose-restricted formula on suspicion; confirm by red-cell GALT activity and/or GALT genotype; treat GALT activity <10%. Lactic acidosis: definitions vary (lactate >4 mmol/L, HCO3 <20, pH <7.35 in one review; MALA confirmed at lactate >5 mmol/L with high-anion-gap acidosis).
explanation.differs: GSD I (glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis both blocked; high lactate) vs GSD III (gluconeogenesis intact; fasting lactate and urate typically normal; milder hypoglycaemia); type A (low tissue oxygen delivery) vs type B (no hypoperfusion) lactic acidosis; reducing sugars (glucose, fructose, lactose, maltose) vs non-reducing sucrose.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: identify GSD I from fasting hypoglycaemia plus high lactate, lipids and urate; choose immediate dietary galactose restriction in a sick newborn; pick the sugar that gives a negative copper-reduction test; classify metformin-associated lactic acidosis as type B; name gluconeogenesis as the dominant glucose source in prolonged fasting.

mnemonic.text: Glucose-6-phosphatase is the liver’s single EXIT DOOR: the glycogen WAREHOUSE and the gluconeogenesis FACTORY both ship glucose through it. Lock the door (GSD I) and the backed-up stock spills into lactate, fat and urate.
mnemonic.explanation: Shows why one enzyme system blocks both fasting pathways and why lactate, lipids and urate rise.
mnemonic.limitation: The kidney also makes and releases glucose; GSD Ib is a translocase (conveyor) defect rather than the door itself; urate rises partly because lactate competes with its renal clearance, not only from backed-up stock; some patients tolerate fasting better than expected, and other tissues carry a related enzyme (G6Pase-beta).

analogyLimitations: Pathways and organs are shown as schematic cards.
Fasting fractions are averages from human tracer studies summarised in one review; individuals vary.
takeaway: After an overnight fast glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis share the work, glycogen storage disease type I blocks the last step of both, suspected galactosaemia means stopping galactose at once, sucrose does not reduce copper, and lactic acidosis is type A with shock and type B without it.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old has marked hepatomegaly, hypoglycaemia a few hours after feeds, high fasting lactate, hypertriglyceridaemia and hyperuricaemia. Glucagon given after a fast produces no rise in glucose and a further rise in lactate. Which defect is most likely?

options.rationale: Correct. The last step of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis is blocked, so glucagon cannot release glucose and glucose-6-phosphate is diverted to lactate.
Incorrect. Gluconeogenesis is intact in GSD III; fasting lactate and uric acid are typically normal.
Incorrect. Galactosaemia presents after milk exposure with vomiting, jaundice, liver damage, sepsis and cataracts, not a glucagon-unresponsive fasting hypoglycaemia with hyperlipidaemia.
Incorrect. This gluconeogenesis defect is a differential, but fasting tolerance is much longer (8–10 hours) and the liver is not as enlarged.

questions.stem: An 8-day-old fed breast milk has vomiting, jaundice, abnormal clotting and Escherichia coli bacteraemia. Classical galactosaemia is suspected. What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Switch immediately to a galactose-restricted formula (soy-based, casein hydrolysate or elemental) while confirmation is pending
options.rationale: Correct. The international guideline recommends starting dietary galactose restriction on suspicion, without waiting for confirmation.

options.text: Continue breast milk until red-cell GALT activity is reported
options.rationale: Incorrect. Galactose restriction, which includes discontinuing breast milk, is what prevents or resolves the acute life-threatening neonatal symptoms, and the guideline says not to wait for confirmation.

options.text: Switch to a whey-based infant formula
options.rationale: Incorrect. Discontinuing breast milk or whey-based formula is part of galactose restriction; whey-based formula is not galactose-restricted.

options.text: Make the diagnosis from a positive urine reducing-substance test alone
options.rationale: Incorrect. Urine reducing substances are non-specific (prematurity, renal tubular acidosis, drugs, other metabolic diseases); confirm with GALT activity and/or GALT gene analysis.

questions.stem: An adult taking metformin has acute kidney injury, blood pressure 120/75 mmHg, normal oxygenation, a high anion gap, pH 7.29 and lactate 6.0 mmol/L. How is this lactic acidosis classified?

options.rationale: Correct. Lactic acidosis without hypoperfusion or hypoxia is type B; metformin (a biguanide) is a B2 cause.
Incorrect. Type A results from low tissue oxygen delivery such as shock; this patient is normotensive and oxygenated.
Incorrect. D-lactic acidosis comes from excess D-lactate made by gut bacteria, typically in short bowel syndrome; nothing here suggests that, whereas metformin is a recognised type B (B2) cause.

options.text: Not lactic acidosis, because lactate is below 10 mmol/L
options.rationale: Incorrect. Lactate 6.0 mmol/L with pH <7.35 and a high anion gap exceeds both the >4 and the >5 mmol/L cut-offs used in the sources.

claims.text: Overnight fast ≈ half glycogenolysis, half gluconeogenesis (lactate, glycerol, amino acids); liver 75–80%, kidney 20–25% by gluconeogenesis only; by 48 h virtually all gluconeogenesis.
GSD I: G6Pase system (Ia enzyme, Ib translocase) blocks the last step of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis; lactate, lipids, urate; glucagon response; contrasts with GSD III and FBPase deficiency.

Classical galactosaemia (GALT): neonatal presentation incl. jaundice, liver damage, E. coli sepsis, cataracts; immediate galactose restriction on suspicion; confirmation by GALT activity/genotype; Q188R population context.
Copper reduction by glucose, fructose, lactose, maltose; sucrose non-reducing; urine reducing substances non-specific.
Lactic acidosis cut-offs vary (>4 or >5 mmol/L, pH <7.35); type A low oxygen delivery; type B1/B2/B3; metformin type B; D-lactate.
Reviewer’s ~12–24 h glycogen supply, “oil-drop” cataracts, Clinitest brand name, anomeric-carbon explanation for sucrose, and lactate >45 mg/dL.
claims.note: Not taught as facts: no open source read in this session states these; the lesson teaches Gerich 2010 fasting fractions, “cataracts”, “copper reduction”, the free-carbonyl mechanism, and mmol/L cut-offs instead.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 17 Hit 11 says GSD Ia is the only glycogen storage disease affecting both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Froissart 2011 attributes the fasting hypoglycaemia of GSD I to blockage of the last step of both pathways by the glucose-6-phosphatase system, which includes the translocase deficient in GSD Ib; Ib shares the block (register flag rv-gsd1-ib-shares-block).

Ch. 17 Hit 12 names Q188R as the galactosaemia mutation without population context. Coelho 2017 and Rubio-Gozalbo 2019: Q188R is the most common variant in people of European ancestry (≈64% of galactosaemic alleles in Caucasian populations); Chinese and Indian populations are largely understudied, so its predominance may not apply to Asian (including Philippine) patients (register flag rv-galt-q188r-population).

Ch. 17 Hit 13 defines lactic acidosis as lactate >5.0 mmol/L with acidaemia. Zanza 2022 states the definition varies in the literature and uses lactate >4 mmol/L, bicarbonate <20 mmol/L and pH <7.35; See 2024 uses >5 mmol/L to confirm metformin-associated lactic acidosis (register flag rv-lactic-acidosis-cutoff).

Ch. 17 Hit 14 says early fasting uses glycogenolysis (~12–24 h supply) and gluconeogenesis takes over once glycogen is gone. Gerich 2010: after a 14–16 h overnight fast about half of released glucose already comes from gluconeogenesis, glycogen is progressively depleted, and virtually all glucose is from gluconeogenesis by 48 h; the 12–24 h figure was not found in sources read (register flag rv-fasting-gng-overlap).
